sources.name: Kevin Powell — Learn Flexbox the easy way

blocks.md: Flexbox is how you put things in a row, space them out, and line them up — you'll reach for it on basically every project. It feels like magic once it clicks.

blocks.canDo: lay out items in a row or column with Flexbox

blocks.md:
**What to focus on** as you watch:

- `display: flex` turns a container into a flex container; its direct children become flex items.
- `justify-content` — spacing along the main axis (left↔right by default).
- `align-items` — alignment on the cross axis (top↔bottom by default).
- `gap` — space between items.
- `flex-direction: row | column` — flips the main axis.

Don't memorise it — get a feel from the video, then *drill it* in the game below until it's automatic.

blocks.title: Learn Flexbox the easy way
blocks.note: Watch the whole thing (~34 min), pausing to try things. Kevin Powell is the best free CSS teacher there is.

blocks.label: 🐸 Now play all 24 levels of Flexbox Froggy — this is where Flexbox actually sticks. ~20 min.

questions.question: On a flex container with the default `flex-direction: row`, which property controls alignment along the horizontal axis?
questions.explanation: `justify-content` operates on the main axis, which runs horizontally in the default row direction.

questions.question: What single CSS declaration do you add to a parent element to make it a flex container?
questions.explanation: `display: flex` on the parent turns it into a flex container and makes all direct children flex items.

questions.question: You set `flex-direction: column` on a container. Which axis does `align-items` now control?
options: It has no effect when direction is column
questions.explanation: Flipping to `flex-direction: column` makes the vertical direction the main axis, so `align-items` then controls alignment horizontally (the cross axis).
